options.explanation: Temperature doesn't provide a deterministic guarantee on a specific numeric business rule; it only nudges general response variability.

keyPrinciple: A hard numeric compliance limit needs a pre-execution interception hook, not a stronger prompt or a post-hoc audit hook — those only observe or reduce, not prevent, the violation.
sourceRef: Exam Guide TS 1.5; Exam Guide §9 Q1; guide_en.md §3.5

stem: Your support agent integrates three backend systems. `get_customer` returns `account_status` as an integer code (`0`, `1`, `2`), `lookup_order` returns `order_status` as a string (`"pending"`, `"shipped"`, `"delivered"`), and a third legacy system returns timestamps as raw Unix epoch integers. In 6% of conversations, the agent misreads `account_status: 2` as if it meant the same thing as a shipped-order status from a different system, giving customers wrong information. What's the most effective fix?

options.text: A system-prompt glossary explaining what each numeric status code and timestamp format means, so the model can translate them itself each time.
options.explanation: A glossary in the prompt still relies on the model correctly applying it fresh on every single turn — the same probabilistic-compliance problem that produced the 6% error rate in the first place.

options.text: A `PostToolUse` hook that normalizes each tool's output into a consistent, clearly labeled format before the model processes any of it.
options.explanation: This is correct: a PostToolUse hook normalizes the data once, deterministically, in code, removing the need for the model to reinterpret formats on every turn.

options.text: A `PreToolUse` hook that blocks any tool call whose result would return a raw integer status code instead of a human-readable string.
options.explanation: Blocking the calls entirely removes functionality the agent needs; the actual need is to transform the data, not prevent it from being returned.

options.text: Consolidate `get_customer` and `lookup_order` into a single combined tool, so agents only ever have to interpret one unified status field.
options.explanation: Merging two backend systems' tools is a larger architectural change than the problem requires, and it doesn't address the third system's raw-timestamp issue at all.

keyPrinciple: Heterogeneous data formats across tools should be normalized once in a PostToolUse hook, not re-interpreted by the model from a prompt glossary on every turn.

stem: Your research coordinator's synthesis subagent occasionally cites sources that were already flagged as retracted or unreliable by an internal source-quality list, because the flag only lives in a spreadsheet a human checks after the report is drafted. You want any subagent's request to fetch content from a flagged source blocked automatically, with the subagent redirected to search for an alternative source instead. Which mechanism fits, and at which point should it act?

options.text: A `PostToolUse` hook that removes flagged sources from search results after they've already been fetched and shown to the subagent.
options.explanation: By the time PostToolUse runs, the fetch has already happened — this is reactive rather than preventing the wasted fetch, and doesn't redirect the subagent to an alternative before it acts on the flagged source.

options.text: A note added to each subagent's `system_prompt` instructing it never to cite sources that appear on the internal retracted/unreliable list.
options.explanation: A prompt instruction is probabilistic; a subagent can still miss it occasionally, and the flagged-source list needs to be checked deterministically against a maintained list, not recalled correctly by the model.

options.text: A human review step placed at the very end of the pipeline that strips citations to flagged sources out of the final report just before it is sent.
options.explanation: Catching this only at final review means flagged citations may already have shaped the subagent's reasoning and the synthesis draft, and doesn't prevent the wasted fetch or downstream reliance on the source.

options.text: An interception hook on the outgoing fetch call that checks the source against the flagged list and blocks or redirects before it executes.
options.explanation: This is correct: a pre-execution interception hook can deterministically block the request and redirect to an alternative before the subagent ever acts on the flagged source.

keyPrinciple: Blocking a specific outgoing tool call before it executes requires a pre-execution interception hook — a post-hoc cleanup step or a prompt reminder only reduces or delays the problem.

stem: You're building a Claude Code workflow that reviews pull requests of varying sizes: some touch 2 files, others touch 20+. Your current implementation always runs a single review pass over the entire diff regardless of size. On PRs with 15+ files, reviewers report that obvious bugs are missed in files reviewed "later" in the pass, and the same pattern is flagged as an issue in one file but approved in another file in the same PR. What restructuring most directly addresses this?

options.text: Split the review into a per-file local-analysis pass for each changed file, plus a separate cross-file integration pass for consistency.
options.explanation: This is correct: separating per-file depth from a dedicated integration pass directly fixes attention dilution while still catching cross-file issues.

options.text: Switch the review to a model with a much larger context window, so the entire diff, however many files it touches, fits comfortably in one single pass.
options.explanation: Attention dilution is about consistency of attention across many files, not whether they technically fit in the context window — a bigger window doesn't guarantee uniform depth of analysis per file.

options.text: Run three independent full-diff review passes and keep only the issues that appear in at least two of the three runs.
options.explanation: Running the same flawed single-pass approach multiple times and requiring consensus can actually suppress real bugs that are only caught intermittently, rather than fixing the underlying dilution.

options.text: Require contributors to split any pull request touching more than 8 files into two or more smaller pull requests before the automated review even runs.
options.explanation: This pushes the problem onto contributors rather than improving the review system itself, and doesn't help for PRs already at or under any chosen threshold that still show inconsistency.

keyPrinciple: Attention dilution across many files is fixed by splitting into a per-file pass plus a separate integration pass — not by a bigger context window or by requiring smaller inputs upstream.
sourceRef: Exam Guide TS 1.6; Exam Guide §9 Q12; guide_en.md §8.3

stem: You're asked to "add comprehensive tests to our 8-year-old billing service, which has almost no test coverage." Before writing any code, a colleague proposes writing a complete, fixed task list up front: "Step 1: write tests for `invoice.py`. Step 2: write tests for `payment.py`. Step 3: write tests for `subscription.py`," listing every file in the module alphabetically. What's the main risk of committing to this fixed plan before investigating the codebase?

options.text: Alphabetical file ordering is a worse choice than starting from the most recently modified file, since recent changes are more likely to still be fresh in mind.
options.explanation: The issue isn't the specific ordering chosen — reordering alphabetically vs. any other fixed order doesn't fix the deeper problem of planning before investigating.

options.text: Fixed, pre-written task lists like this one cannot actually be executed by Claude Code at all — only an interactively-guided human developer can follow one.
options.explanation: This is false — fixed task lists can absolutely be executed; the real issue is whether a fixed list is the right strategy for a task whose scope is unknown up front.

options.text: The plan doesn't reflect actual risk or coverage gaps, and can't adapt to hidden dependencies discovered only once you start investigating.
options.explanation: This is correct: a fixed pre-investigation plan can't reflect risk priority or adapt to dependencies discovered only once you actually explore the codebase.

options.text: The plan violates the principle that all subagent prompts must specify goals rather than steps.
options.explanation: That principle applies to subagent delegation prompts, not to whether a top-level task itself should be decomposed adaptively vs. via a fixed pipeline.

keyPrinciple: Open-ended, investigation-dependent work (like adding tests to an unfamiliar legacy codebase) needs dynamic adaptive decomposition — map structure and risk first, then build and adjust a prioritized plan — not a fixed list committed to before any exploration.

stem: Your team runs two different kinds of Claude Code automation: (1) a weekly "generate the changelog from merged PRs" task that always follows the same five steps in the same order, and (2) an ad hoc "investigate why the checkout flow got slower this release" task, where the actual cause is unknown and each finding determines where to look next. A new team member proposes using dynamic adaptive decomposition for both, arguing consistency is good practice everywhere. What's the issue with applying it to the changelog task?

options.text: Dynamic adaptive decomposition cannot be applied to any task that runs on a fixed schedule, since scheduled automation requires a fully pre-written plan.
options.explanation: This is false — a task's schedule (weekly vs. ad hoc) doesn't determine which decomposition strategy fits; the deciding factor is whether the task's structure is predictable.

options.text: The changelog task's steps are fully predictable and identical every run, so a fixed pipeline is simpler than adaptively re-planning each run.
options.explanation: This is correct: a task with fully known, repeating structure is exactly what a fixed pipeline is designed for, without the overhead of adaptive re-planning.

options.text: Fixed pipelines always produce higher-quality output than dynamic decomposition, regardless of task type.
options.explanation: Neither pattern is universally higher quality; the right choice is about matching the pattern to the task's predictability, not a blanket ranking of one over the other.

options.text: Applying dynamic decomposition to the changelog task would require giving it access to the `Task` tool so it could spawn subagents to investigate each PR.
options.explanation: Adaptive decomposition is a planning strategy applied in code or prompting, not something that inherently requires subagent spawning via Task.

keyPrinciple: Match the decomposition strategy to how predictable the task's structure is — a fixed, repeating task doesn't benefit from dynamic re-planning overhead.

stem: You spent yesterday investigating a flaky checkout test using a named session: `claude --resume checkout-flake-investigation`. You found the root cause was a race condition in `cart_sync.ts` and documented the fix approach, but didn't implement it. Overnight, a teammate's unrelated PR merged and modified `cart_sync.ts` (changing unrelated logic higher in the file) and two other files you had read during the investigation. This morning you resume the same named session and simply say "go ahead and implement the fix we discussed." What's the main risk of doing this without saying more?

options.text: `--resume` with a session name only works once; using it a second time on the same session name will silently start a brand-new, empty session.
options.explanation: This is false — named sessions can be resumed multiple times; this isn't a real limitation of --resume.

options.text: Resuming a named session after any file anywhere in the repository has changed will cause the CLI to detect the mismatch and refuse to resume, throwing an error.
options.explanation: This is false — resuming doesn't automatically detect or block on file changes; the CLI proceeds with prior context regardless, which is exactly the risk.

options.text: The fix approach documented yesterday will be automatically discarded the moment a resumed session detects new git commits since the session was last active.
options.explanation: This is false — nothing about resuming automatically discards prior findings based on git activity; the actual risk is the opposite, stale results being silently trusted rather than discarded.

options.text: The agent may reason from its earlier `Read` results for `cart_sync.ts`, which no longer reflect the file's current contents after the merge.
options.explanation: This is correct: without being told what changed, the resumed agent may trust stale Read results and implement the fix against outdated file contents.

keyPrinciple: Resuming a session after underlying files changed risks the agent reasoning from stale prior tool results unless you explicitly tell it what changed.

stem: After a shared codebase investigation (mapping the state-management module and its dependents), you want to compare two different refactor approaches — one using Redux, one using React Context — without redoing the shared mapping work twice, and while keeping both explorations available to return to independently. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Use `fork_session` to branch two independent sessions from the completed investigation's shared context, one per refactor approach.
options.explanation: This is correct: fork_session branches independent sessions from a shared baseline, avoiding duplicated groundwork while keeping both paths available separately.

options.text: Resume the same named session twice, in two separate terminal windows at once, giving each window a different approach in mind but never actually forking.
options.explanation: Resuming the identical session in parallel doesn't create two independent, divergent histories — both "branches" would be writing into the same session state rather than diverging cleanly the way a fork does.

options.text: Start two entirely new sessions from scratch, each re-running the full codebase investigation before exploring its respective approach.
options.explanation: This discards the entire benefit of the shared baseline by re-running the identical investigation work twice, which is exactly what forking from a shared baseline avoids.

options.text: Use `--resume` once, complete the Redux approach fully end to end, then resume that same session again afterward to explore the Context API approach.
options.explanation: Doing the approaches sequentially in the same session means the Context API exploration happens with the Redux approach's decisions already baked in, rather than diverging cleanly from the shared baseline, and loses the ability to keep both explorations available independently.

keyPrinciple: fork_session branches two independent explorations from one shared analysis baseline, avoiding duplicated groundwork while keeping both paths available separately.

stem: Three weeks ago, you used Claude Code to do a deep investigation of a legacy monolith's module boundaries in preparation for a microservices migration, spanning many `Read` and `Grep` calls across dozens of files, saved as a named session. Since then, roughly 30% of the files you investigated have been modified by ongoing feature work, and the investigation session has grown very long. You now need to resume the migration planning. What's generally the more reliable approach at this point?

options.text: Resume the old named session exactly as-is, on the reasoning that three full weeks of accumulated investigation context outweighs the risk from a partial set of file changes.
options.explanation: With roughly a third of the investigated files changed and significant time elapsed, much of that accumulated context is now stale tool output the agent could mistakenly trust — quantity of context isn't the deciding factor, accuracy is.

options.text: Resume the old named session, but before doing anything else ask the agent to re-read every single file it ever touched across the entire session.
options.explanation: Re-reading every file discards the efficiency benefit of the prior investigation entirely, re-doing full exploration when only some files actually changed and a structured summary could convey what's still valid far more cheaply.

options.text: Start a fresh session and inject a concise, accurate summary of the prior findings into the first prompt, instead of resuming the full stale history.
options.explanation: This is correct: with substantial staleness and a long elapsed time, a fresh session with an accurate summary is more reliable than carrying forward a large amount of now-partly-outdated context.

options.text: Fork the old session into a new branch, then treat the fork as equivalent to a fresh session with accurate current context.
options.explanation: Forking still carries forward the same stale tool-call history from the shared baseline — it doesn't refresh anything or resolve staleness, since both the fork and the original inherit the same partly outdated prior context.

keyPrinciple: When a large share of prior tool results are stale after significant time and file changes, starting fresh with an accurate structured summary is more reliable than resuming or forking a session carrying that stale context forward.
